prompt: By Grove’s sum, what is a manager’s output?
hint: Two terms, and neither is the manager’s own work.

choices.text: The work they still do with their own hands
choices.why: That is the old ruler. Grove’s sum leaves the manager’s own work out unless it changes what the team produces.

choices.text: The number of decisions they make in a week, weighted by what each one costs
choices.why: A decision counts only through what it changes in the team’s output; a count of decisions measures activity.

choices.text: Their team’s output plus that of neighbouring teams they influence
choices.why: Right: the sum has two terms, the organisation and the neighbours under its influence, and nothing the manager does alone.

choices.text: Their team’s output alone
choices.why: Half of it. The second term, the neighbouring teams under the manager’s influence, is as much part of the job.

prompt: Renata persuades the Payments team to expose an endpoint a quarter early, and Agenda ships a feature sooner as a result. Where does that appear in Grove’s sum?
hint: Who did the extra work, and whose output went up?

choices.text: Nowhere, because she wrote no code
choices.why: That measures her by commits, the ruler the lesson says belongs to the old job.

choices.text: Only in the Payments team’s output, since they built the endpoint
choices.why: They built it, but the point of persuading them was what it let Agenda ship sooner.

choices.text: In both terms: her influence on a neighbour raised her own team’s output
choices.why: Right. Payments is a neighbour under her influence, and the result is that Agenda’s output rose without anybody on it working harder.

choices.text: As her personal output for the quarter
choices.why: The sum has no personal term at all; the conversation counts through what the team then delivered.

prompt: In her second week Renata takes a small ticket because nobody else is free. By Wednesday two people are waiting on her decisions and the ticket is still open. What does the lesson draw from it?
hint: Is the problem the code, or the reason she picked it up?

choices.text: A manager should never write code
choices.why: Lesson 2 describes a shape of the role where code is part of the job, so the lesson does not say this.

choices.text: Code is now a choice, and comfort is a poor reason for it
choices.why: Right. The lesson says code is not wrong for a manager; the reason matters, and comfort is a reason that costs the team.

choices.text: The ticket was too large for somebody with meetings
choices.why: It was small; size was not what went wrong, the decisions left waiting were.

choices.text: She should have asked Otávio before picking up a ticket in her first month
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson makes this a question of permission; it is about where her hours multiply.

prompt: Match each thing that moves with the lessons that deal with it.

pairs.right: delegating outcomes and deciding how much freedom goes with them
the one-to-one, the meeting that fixes what people stop telling you
feedback, promotion and the hard conversations

right_distractors: the deploy pipeline and the on-call rota

prompt: Why does a team meeting at 11:00 cost more than it looks?
hint: Think of the people in it, not the hour.

choices.text: Meetings before lunch run longer than meetings after it
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about length; the cost is where the meeting falls in a maker’s day.

choices.text: Managers are least productive at that hour
choices.why: The cost falls on the engineers, whose long blocks it breaks, not on the manager.

choices.text: It cuts every attendee’s morning in half
choices.why: Right: seven engineers lose seven unbroken mornings, which is why the team moved its regular meetings to the edges of the day.

choices.text: It leaves twenty-minute gaps in the manager’s calendar that are too short to use for anything
choices.why: Those gaps are real, but they are a cost of the manager’s own fragmented day, not of this meeting.

prompt: Which of these answers its question soonest?
hint: Place each on the figure’s axis.

choices.text: Feedback given in a one-to-one
choices.why: Whether feedback worked shows over the following weeks, when the behaviour changes or not.

choices.text: A promotion case written today
choices.why: It is decided at the next review cycle, about six months away at Caju.

choices.text: A code review
choices.why: Right: a review answers the same day, hours rather than weeks.

choices.text: A hire made this month
choices.why: A hire shows whether it was right somewhere between three months and a year.

prompt: Agenda ships a strong first quarter under Renata. Why should she not conclude that her changes worked?
hint: What else could explain a good quarter?

choices.text: One quarter is always too short to measure any team
choices.why: Teams can be measured over a quarter; what one quarter cannot show is the effect of a new manager’s choices.

choices.text: Good results usually mean the team is being pushed too hard
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson links good results to pressure; the point is about attribution.

choices.text: Results only count once the next review cycle has looked at them and confirmed them
choices.why: A review cycle is one of the long loops, but nothing makes results invisible until it runs.

choices.text: The quarter may run on decisions made before she arrived
choices.why: Right: with loops this long, luck and the previous manager’s work cannot yet be told apart from her own.

prompt: Paul Graham’s essay contrasts the maker’s schedule with the ___ schedule.
hint: The other person in the essay’s title.

prompt: Which listening-tour question does the lesson say people skip, and matters most?
hint: A new manager arrives looking for problems.

choices.text: What is getting in your way?
choices.why: People answer this one readily; it finds problems, which a new manager is already looking for.

choices.text: If you were in my seat, what would you change first?
choices.why: Useful, but it points at change, and the risk the lesson names is breaking what works.

choices.text: What is going well that I should be careful not to break?
choices.why: Right: it is what surfaced Diego’s fast reviews, which Renata had been about to cut back.

choices.text: What do you need from me?
choices.why: A good question, though not the one the lesson singles out as skipped.

prompt: In Renata’s table, how many more people raised the dependency on Payments than raised the slow pipeline?
Why did Renata ask the two people who built the old on-call rota to draft the new one?
hint: An early change can be read as something.

choices.text: Because a manager should not spend time on rotas
choices.why: The lesson does not rank rotas below the manager; it is about how the change is received.

choices.text: Because they were the two people who had covered the most holidays under the old rota
choices.why: Five people raised the problem; the two were chosen because they had designed the old rota.

choices.text: To delay the change until after her first ninety days
choices.why: She made the change inside the window, in the second month, on purpose.

choices.text: So the change became their project rather than a verdict on their work
choices.why: Right: the lesson warns that early changes read as verdicts, and handing the redesign to its authors avoids that.

prompt: What does the course ask you to install?
hint: Look at what the practice is made of.

choices.text: Nothing beyond somewhere to write and count
choices.why: Right. LibreOffice is recommended, but a plain text file and paper are enough to do every task.

choices.text: An HR system to practise performance reviews in
choices.why: No lesson uses one; every template is written out in the lesson that needs it.

choices.text: A shared drive where the notebook lives
choices.why: The opposite: the notebook holds personal data and belongs where only you can open it.

choices.text: A video-call tool, for the practice one-to-ones
choices.why: The practice is scenario questions and written tasks; there are no calls.

prompt: Thiago tells Renata he needs Thursdays flexible for two months because of a medical treatment. What goes in her notebook?
hint: Write what you need to act on.

choices.text: The treatment, so she can follow up on how he is
choices.why: Caring about him does not need a medical record in her notes, and the law treats it as sensitive.

choices.text: Nothing, since personal matters never belong in work notes
choices.why: The request itself is something she has to act on and remember, so it belongs there.

choices.text: A note in the team wiki, so others can cover Thursdays
choices.why: The team may need to know there is cover to arrange; it does not need his reasons, and the wiki is shared.

choices.text: The request and its dates, without the medical reason
choices.why: Right: health information is sensitive personal data, and the action needs only the request.

prompt: Put the four parts of the notebook in the order the lesson lists them.
hint: Who, then what was decided, then what was promised, then the writing.

prompt: A newly promoted manager says: “I spent the whole week in meetings and got nothing done, so next week I’m blocking two days to clear my tickets.” What would you check first?
hint: What is “got nothing done” measured against?

choices.text: Which of those meetings changed what the team produces
choices.why: Right: by Grove’s sum the week may have been productive, and two days on tickets may cost the team more than they return.

choices.text: Whether two days is enough to clear the tickets
choices.why: That accepts his ruler, commits and tickets, which is the one the lesson says the job no longer uses.

choices.text: Whether he could decline all his meetings next week instead of just most of them
choices.why: Some of those meetings are the job; cutting all of them assumes the meetings were the waste.

choices.text: Whether his manager approves the blocked days
choices.why: Approval does not answer whether the days are well spent, which is the question.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for not changing things in a new manager’s first weeks? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: She knows the problems from one seat
choices.why: Yes: the platform migration and Helena’s use of planning were invisible from where she sat.

choices.text: Early changes are read as verdicts
choices.why: Yes: changing the rota in week one would have told its authors their work was wrong.

choices.text: Changes made early are harder to undo
choices.why: The lesson does not argue reversibility here; its reasons are about knowledge and how a change is read.

choices.text: She has no record of what people told her yet
choices.why: Yes: after a month she can say what she heard; in week one only what she thinks.

choices.text: A new manager has no authority to change anything for ninety days
choices.why: She had the authority from the first week; the lesson is about using it well.
